items.title: No shift-level measurement of screening on this ward
items.whyItMatters: One week of notes cannot show where screening fails across shifts, weekdays and patient groups.
items.opportunity: Reconcile screening entries with ward lists for every patient-shift for 12 weeks.

items.title: Documentation overstates screening
items.whyItMatters: About one documented screen in six was not performed elsewhere (claim c2).
items.opportunity: Observe a sample of shifts, including two night shifts a week, to estimate how many recorded screens were done.

items.title: People with dementia or sensory loss screened least
items.whyItMatters: The groups at highest risk are screened least often (claim c3).
items.opportunity: Pre-specify dementia, sensory loss and side rooms as patient groups for the analysis.

items.title: The step from positive screen to review is unmeasured
items.whyItMatters: A positive screen that waits a day changes little for the patient (claim c4).
items.opportunity: Record the time from each positive screen to documented medical review.

items.title: Observation could change what it measures
items.whyItMatters: Nurses who know they are observed may screen more on sampled shifts.
items.opportunity: Compare record-based completion on observed and unobserved shifts.

errorsFound: The spot check counted documented screens as performed; the retrieved evidence shows that assumption overestimates screening.
reevaluation: The gaps support a descriptive prospective observational design with full record reconciliation, a sample of direct observation and the review step measured, before any improvement is chosen.
summary: Five gaps: no shift-level data, inflated documentation, inequity by patient group, the unmeasured review step and observer effect.
